Lacking modern arms and international backing, the insurrection was ruthlessly crushed within days by the Burundian national army, sparking extensive retaliatory killings throughout the region. \n\n Status: Unrecognised secessionist state; Administrative seat: Makamba; Common languages: Kirundi and French; Government: Insurgent revolutionary committee; Historical era: Ikiza; Established: 5 May 1972; Disestablished: 1 June 1972; Preceded by: Republic of Burundi; Succeeded by: Republic of Burundi

name: United Republic of Cameroon
description: The United Republic of Cameroon came into existence on 20 May 1972 following a national referendum that abolished the previous federal system to consolidate unitary rule under President Ahmadou Ahidjo. Governed from the inland capital of Yaoundé, the Central African state centralised political decision-making, gradually submerging the administrative distinctiveness of the anglophone western regions. Following Ahidjo's unexpected resignation in November 1982, power transferred to his constitutional successor Paul Biya, who further unified executive control before dropping United from the country's official name in 1984. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Yaoundé; Largest city: Douala; Official languages: French and English; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Head of state: Ahmadou Ahidjo; Legislature: National Assembly; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 20 May 1972; Reorganised: 1984; Currency: Central African CFA franc

name: Republic of Sri Lanka
description: The Republic of Sri Lanka was established on 22 May 1972 when Ceylon severed its remaining constitutional connections with the British Crown and enacted a new republican charter under Prime Minister Sirimavo Bandaranaike. Administered from Colombo on the south-western coast, the state elevated Sinhala as the dominant official language and enshrined Buddhism, which heightened political alienation among the Tamil minority. The left-leaning coalition government implemented socialist economic nationalisations until the United National Party won power in 1977, adopting a presidential system in September 1978. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital and largest city: Colombo; Official languages: Sinhala and Tamil; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Unitary parliamentary republic; Head of government: Sirimavo Bandaranaike; Legislature: National State Assembly; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 22 May 1972; Disestablished: 7 September 1978; Currency: Sri Lankan rupee

name: Bophuthatswana
label: bantustans
description: Bophuthatswana was a Bantustan designated by the South African apartheid government for the Tswana people, receiving self-governing status on 1 June 1972 and nominal independence in December 1977. Administered from Mmabatho, the unrecognised state consisted of seven discontinuous territorial fragments scattered across three South African provinces. Governed autocratically by President Lucas Mangope and bolstered financially by Sun City casino revenues and platinum mines, the homeland collapsed following popular revolts and military mutinies before reincorporation into South Africa in April 1994. \n\n Status: Bantustan puppet state; Capital and largest city: Mmabatho; Official languages: Setswana, English and Afrikaans; Government: Nominally presidential republic; Head of state: Lucas Mangope; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Apartheid era; Established: 1 June 1972; Disestablished: 27 April 1994; Currency: South African rand

name: Lebowa
label: bantustans
description: Lebowa was an apartheid-era homeland established in the north-eastern Transvaal for the Northern Sotho and Pedi populations, receiving internal self-governing status on 2 October 1972. Operating initially from Seshego before transferring its administration to the purpose-built capital of Lebowakgomo, the non-contiguous territory was led for much of its history by Chief Minister Cedric Phatudi. The homeland government opposed full nominal independence from Pretoria while administering severely overcrowded rural tracts until the territory was dismantled and absorbed into South Africa's Limpopo province in 1994. \n\n Status: Bantustan homeland; Capital: Lebowakgomo; Common languages: Northern Sotho, English and Afrikaans; Government: Subordinate ethnic administration; Head of state: Cedric Phatudi; Historical era: Apartheid era; Established: 2 October 1972; Disestablished: 27 April 1994; Currency: South African rand

name: East Caprivi
label: bantustans
description: East Caprivi, also known as Itenge, was an ethnic homeland established in 1973 within the strategic Caprivi Strip of eastern South West Africa under South Africa's separate development scheme. Administered from Katima Mulilo on the Zambezi River, the territory was designated for the Masubiya and Mafwe communities and granted self-governing status in 1976. Due to its strategic location bordering Angola, Zambia and Botswana, the area was heavily garrisoned by the South African military before its administrative structures were dissolved in June 1989. \n\n Status: Bantustan homeland; Administrative seat: Katima Mulilo; Common languages: Lozi, Subiya, Afrikaans and English; Government: Subordinate ethnic administration; Historical era: Apartheid era; Established: 1973; Disestablished: 1 June 1989; Succeeded by: Republic of Namibia; Currency: South African rand

name: Gazankulu
label: bantustans
description: Gazankulu was created as a self-governing Bantustan on 1 February 1973 in the northern and eastern Transvaal, set aside by the apartheid regime for the Tsonga and Shangaan peoples. Headquartered at the administrative centre of Giyani, the homeland comprised several fragmented parcels of territory bordered by Lebowa and Kruger National Park. Led throughout most of its existence by Chief Minister Hudson Ntsanwisi, the administration consistently refused nominal independence, remaining an unrecognised dependent entity until its reintegration into South Africa on 27 April 1994. \n\n Status: Bantustan homeland; Administrative seat: Giyani; Common languages: Tsonga, English and Afrikaans; Government: Subordinate ethnic administration; Head of state: Hudson Ntsanwisi; Historical era: Apartheid era; Established: 1 February 1973; Disestablished: 27 April 1994; Currency: South African rand

name: Republic of Venda
label: bantustans
description: The Republic of Venda was designated as a self-governing homeland on 1 February 1973 and subsequently proclaimed nominally independent by South Africa on 13 September 1979. Situated in the Soutpansberg region of northern Transvaal near the Zimbabwean border, the entity was governed from Thohoyandou for the Venda people. Under President Patrick Mphephu and his successor Frank Ravele, the regime enforced one-party rule until overthrown by a military coup in 1990, after which the isolated enclave was reabsorbed into South Africa in April 1994. \n\n Status: Bantustan puppet state; Capital and largest city: Thohoyandou; Official languages: Venda; Common languages: English and Afrikaans; Government: Nominally presidential republic; Head of state: Patrick Mphephu; Legislature: Legislative Assembly; Historical era: Apartheid era; Established: 1 February 1973; Disestablished: 27 April 1994; Currency: South African rand

name: Belize
description: Belize was formally renamed on 1 June 1973 when the self-governing British colony previously known as British Honduras adopted its indigenous title ahead of full national sovereignty. Headquartered at the newly established interior capital of Belmopan following the devastation of Belize City by Hurricane Hattie, the Central American territory was led by Premier George Cadle Price. Despite protracted territorial claims and military invasion threats from neighbouring Guatemala that required a permanent British garrison, the colony achieved complete sovereign independence as a Commonwealth realm on 21 September 1981. \n\n Status: Self-governing British crown colony; Capital: Belmopan; Largest city: Belize City; Official languages: English; Common languages: Belizean Creole and Spanish; Government: Parliamentary dependency under constitutional monarchy; Head of government: George Cadle Price; Historical era: Decolonisation; Established: 1 June 1973; Disestablished: 21 September 1981; Currency: Belize dollar

name: Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya (Military Occupation)
description: The Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya Military Occupation comprised the northern Chadian border territory known as the Aouzou Strip, occupied and annexed by Libyan armed forces in 1973. Administered directly by Libyan military authorities from garrisons linked to Tripoli, the mineral-rich Saharan salient was claimed by Muammar Gaddafi under a disputed 1935 Franco-Italian treaty. Libyan forces fortified the region with airbases and supported Chadian rebel factions until being routed and decisively expelled by Chadian forces during the Toyota War in September 1987. \n\n Status: Military occupation administration; Capital: Tripoli; Common languages: Arabic and French; Government: Military administrative command; Head of state: Muammar Gaddafi; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 1 July 1973; Disestablished: 1 September 1987; Preceded by: Republic of Chad; Succeeded by: Republic of Chad

name: Commonwealth of The Bahamas
description: The Commonwealth of The Bahamas attained sovereign statehood on 10 July 1973, concluding over three centuries of British colonial administration across the Lucayan Archipelago. Governed from Nassau on the island of New Providence, the Atlantic archipelagic realm retained Queen Elizabeth II as constitutional monarch, represented by a governor-general, with domestic affairs directed by founding prime minister Lynden Pindling. The nation developed a thriving economy based on high-end tourism and offshore banking, maintaining durable parliamentary traditions and multi-party elections across its hundreds of inhabited islands and cays. \n\n Status: Commonwealth realm; Capital and largest city: Nassau; Official languages: English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Head of state: Monarch of the United Kingdom; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Contemporary; Currency: Bahamian dollar

name: Republic of Afghanistan
description: The Republic of Afghanistan was first established on 17 July 1973 when former prime minister Mohammed Daoud Khan overthrew King Mohammad Zahir Shah in a bloodless coup, abolishing the monarchy. Operating from Kabul, Daoud instituted an authoritarian republican regime focused on economic modernisation and non-aligned diplomacy until his death during the communist Saur Revolution in 1978. The republican title was restored in December 1987 under President Mohammad Najibullah as part of national reconciliation reforms, enduring through the Soviet military withdrawal until the regime collapsed to Mujahideen forces in April 1992. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital and largest city: Kabul; Official languages: Pashto and Dari; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Head of state: Mohammed Daoud Khan; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 17 July 1973; Disestablished: 15 April 1992; Currency: Afghan afghani

name: Republic of Guinea-Bissau
description: The Republic of Guinea-Bissau unilaterally declared its sovereign independence on 24 September 1973 in the liberated interior settlement of Madina do Boe, culminating an eleven-year armed struggle against Portuguese colonial rule led by the PAIGC. Operating from the coastal capital of Bissau following Portuguese recognition in 1974, the young socialist republic was guided by founding president Luis Cabral. Despite subsequent decades marked by recurring military coups and institutional fragility, the West African nation preserved its hard-won sovereignty, relying primarily on cashew farming, fishing and agricultural exports. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Bissau; Official languages: Portuguese; Common languages: Guinea-Bissau Creole; Religion: Islam, Christianity and traditional faiths; Government: Unitary semi-presidential republic; Legislature: National People's Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Currency: West African CFA franc

name: Portuguese Republic
description: The Portuguese Republic was comprehensively reconstituted on 25 April 1974 when the Carnation Revolution bloodlessly toppled the decades-old Estado Novo dictatorship in Lisbon. Guided by the Armed Forces Movement, the Iberian nation swiftly dismantled its overseas empire in Africa and Asia, ending prolonged colonial wars and establishing a progressive constitutional democracy. Enacting a new democratic constitution in 1976, Portugal integrated rapidly with Western Europe, joining the European Economic Community in 1986 and modernising its civil institutions, public infrastructure and commercial economy. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Lisbon; Official languages: Portuguese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary semi-presidential republic; Legislature: Assembly of the Republic; Historical era: Contemporary; Preceded by: Estado Novo; Currency: Euro

name: United Nations Buffer Zone in Cyprus
description: The United Nations Buffer Zone in Cyprus was permanently consolidated on 16 August 1974 following the ceasefire that concluded the Turkish military invasion and partition of the island. Patrolled continuously by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus without civil municipal sovereignty, the demilitarised strip stretches approximately one hundred and eighty kilometres from Kato Pyrgos in the west to Famagusta in the east. Also known as the Green Line, the corridor bisects the historic walled city of Nicosia, maintaining military disengagement and facilitating humanitarian coordination across the divided territory. \n\n Status: United Nations demilitarised buffer zone; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: UNFICYP headquarters; Common languages: English, Greek and Turkish; Government: Multilateral peacekeeping administration; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 16 August 1974

name: Niue
description: Niue achieved self-governing status in free association with New Zealand on 19 October 1974 following a constitutional referendum approved by its Polynesian inhabitants. Governed from the coastal village of Alofi, the isolated uplifted coral atoll exercises full legislative and executive authority through the Niue Assembly, while New Zealand provides requested assistance with defence and external diplomacy. Retaining King Charles III as head of state and using the New Zealand dollar, Niue maintains vibrant Polynesian cultural traditions alongside extensive diaspora ties in Auckland. \n\n Status: Self-governing state in free association; Capital and largest settlement: Alofi; Official languages: Niuean and English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Head of state: Monarch of New Zealand; Legislature: Niue Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Currency: New Zealand dollar

name: QwaQwa
label: bantustans
description: QwaQwa was an ethnic homeland established on 1 November 1974 in the eastern Orange Free State by the South African apartheid government for the Sesotho-speaking Basotho people. Centred at Phuthaditjhaba, formerly known as Witsieshoek, near the Maloti Mountains bordering Lesotho, the territory encompassed an extraordinarily small area of just six hundred and fifty-five square kilometres. Ruled for two decades by Chief Minister Kenneth Mopeli, the impoverished and severely overpopulated enclave rejected nominal independence before being abolished and reintegrated into South Africa on 27 April 1994. \n\n Status: Bantustan homeland; Administrative seat: Phuthaditjhaba; Common languages: Sesotho, Afrikaans and English; Government: Subordinate ethnic administration; Head of state: Kenneth Mopeli; Historical era: Apartheid era; Established: 1 November 1974; Disestablished: 27 April 1994; Currency: South African rand

name: Republic of Malta
description: The Republic of Malta was proclaimed on 13 December 1974 when the strategic Mediterranean archipelago adopted a republican constitution, replacing Queen Elizabeth II with an indigenous presidency under Sir Anthony Mamo. Administered from the historic fortified capital of Valletta, the young republic closed the permanent British naval base in 1979 under Prime Minister Dom Mintoff to establish a policy of strict international neutrality. Over subsequent decades, Malta leveraged its Mediterranean shipping lanes, financial services and tourism before joining the European Union in May 2004. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Valletta; Largest city: Birkirkara; Official languages: Maltese and English; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary parliamentary republic; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Contemporary; Currency: Euro

name: Socialist Republic of the Union of Burma
description: The Socialist Republic of the Union of Burma was officially instituted under a new socialist constitution that codified the one-party rule of General Ne Win and the Burma Socialist Programme Party. Administered from the riverine capital of Rangoon, the regime pursued the idiosyncratic Burmese Way to Socialism, blending Soviet-style central planning, strict Buddhist philosophical tenets and extreme diplomatic isolation. Widespread economic ruin, demonetisation scandals and escalating popular unrest culminated in the massive 8888 Uprising, which was brutally suppressed when armed forces seized direct control on 18 September 1988. \n\n Status: Sovereign socialist republic; Capital and largest city: Rangoon; Official languages: Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: One-party socialist military dictatorship; Head of state: Ne Win; Legislature: Pyithu Hluttaw; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 2 March 1974; Disestablished: 18 September 1988; Currency: Burmese kyat

name: Turkish Federated State of Cyprus
description: The Turkish Federated State of Cyprus was proclaimed on 13 February 1975 across northern Cyprus by the Turkish Cypriot leadership under Rauf Denktas following the Turkish military intervention. Centred in North Nicosia, the administration was conceived not as an independent country but as a self-governing constituent component for a proposed future bicommunal federation on the island. Due to the complete collapse of bilateral negotiations with the Greek Cypriot government, the federated entity was reconstituted on 15 November 1983 as the sovereign Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. \n\n Status: Partially recognised federated state; Capital and largest city: North Nicosia; Official languages: Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Semi-presidential republic; Head of state: Rauf Denktas; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 13 February 1975; Disestablished: 15 November 1983; Currency: Turkish lira

name: Provisional Military Government of Socialist Ethiopia
description: The Provisional Military Government of Socialist Ethiopia, widely known as the Derg, officially abolished the ancient Ethiopian monarchy on 21 March 1975 to establish a Marxist-Leninist military state. Governed from Addis Ababa on the central Ethiopian plateau, the regime was led by Mengistu Haile Mariam, who nationalised rural lands, collectivised agriculture and brutally eliminated political rivals during the Red Terror. Heavily supported by Soviet weaponry and Cuban troops during the 1977 Ogaden War, the Derg governed by martial decree until promulgating a civilianised constitution in February 1987. \n\n Status: Sovereign socialist state; Capital and largest city: Addis Ababa; Official languages: Amharic; Religion: State atheism; Government: Provisional communist military junta; Head of state: Mengistu Haile Mariam; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 21 March 1975; Disestablished: 22 February 1987; Currency: Ethiopian birr

name: Kampuchea
description: Kampuchea was the transitional revolutionary state established on 17 April 1975 when the Khmer Rouge seized Phnom Penh, terminating the Khmer Republic in the Cambodian Civil War. Functioning under the nominal leadership of Prince Norodom Sihanouk and the National United Front of Kampuchea, true power resided with Pol Pot and the secretive Communist Party of Kampuchea. The regime immediately emptied urban centres, force-marched millions into agrarian labour communes and initiated radical social transformations before promulgating the official constitution of Democratic Kampuchea on 5 January 1976. \n\n Status: Sovereign revolutionary state; Capital and largest city: Phnom Penh; Official languages: Khmer; Religion: State atheism; Government: Totalitarian communist regime; Head of state: Norodom Sihanouk; Head of government: Penn Nouth; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 17 April 1975; Disestablished: 5 January 1976; Succeeded by: Democratic Kampuchea

name: People's Republic of Mozambique
description: The People's Republic of Mozambique was established on 25 June 1975 when the southern African territory attained sovereign independence from Portugal under the leadership of FRELIMO. Governed from the coastal capital of Lourenco Marques, promptly renamed Maputo, the state was led by President Samora Machel, who adopted Marxist-Leninism and allied with the Soviet Union. The republic soon confronted a destructive fifteen-year civil war against RENAMO insurgents backed by neighbouring Rhodesia and South Africa, which persisted until political liberalisation and a new democratic constitution were adopted in November 1990. \n\n Status: Sovereign socialist state; Capital and largest city: Maputo; Official languages: Portuguese; Religion: State atheism; Government: Unitary socialist republic; Head of state: Samora Machel; Legislature: People's Assembly; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 25 June 1975; Disestablished: 30 November 1990; Currency: Mozambican metical

name: Republic of Cabo Verde
description: The Republic of Cabo Verde achieved sovereign independence from Portugal on 5 July 1975, ending five centuries of colonial administration across the Atlantic volcanic archipelago. Governed from Praia on Santiago Island, the young island nation was initially led by President Aristides Pereira under a shared revolutionary framework with Guinea-Bissau. Despite severe arid conditions and limited natural resources, Cabo Verde successfully established one of Africa's most stable constitutional democracies in the early 1990s, fostering economic resilience through tourism, maritime logistics and international services. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Praia; Official languages: Portuguese; Common languages: Cape Verdean Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary semi-presidential republic; Legislature: National Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Currency: Cape Verdean escudo

name: State of Comoros
description: The State of Comoros emerged on 6 July 1975 when the volcanic Indian Ocean archipelago unilaterally proclaimed independence from France under President Ahmed Abdallah, excluding the island of Mayotte. Governed from Moroni on Grande Comore, the state suffered immediate upheaval when socialist politician Ali Soilih seized power with the aid of French mercenary Bob Denard. Soilih launched radical revolutionary programmes to dismantle traditional Islamic and feudal customs until another mercenary-led coup deposed him in May 1978, leading to the creation of the Federal Islamic Republic of the Comoros. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Moroni; Official languages: Comorian, French and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Revolutionary republic; Head of state: Ali Soilih; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 6 July 1975; Disestablished: 23 October 1978; Succeeded by: Federal Islamic Republic of the Comoros; Currency: Comorian franc

name: Democratic Republic of São Tomé and Príncipe
description: The Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe gained sovereign statehood on 12 July 1975, concluding five centuries of Portuguese colonial rule over the equatorial Gulf of Guinea islands. Administered from Sao Tome on the larger island, the newly independent nation operated initially as a one-party socialist state under President Manuel Pinto da Costa and the MLSTP. Following national democratic conferences in 1990, the country transitioned smoothly into a peaceful multi-party constitutional democracy, sustaining its economy through cocoa cultivation, fishing and burgeoning ecotourism. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Sao Tome; Official languages: Portuguese; Common languages: Forro Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary semi-presidential republic; Legislature: National Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Currency: Dobra

name: Republic of the North Solomons
description: The Republic of the North Solomons was an unrecognised secessionist state declared on 1 September 1975 by leaders on Bougainville Island, just two weeks before Papua New Guinea attained independence from Australia. Centred at Kieta and Arawa, the separatist government was led by President Alexis Sarei, who sought self-determination to retain lucrative revenues from the Panguna copper mine. Lacking international recognition and diplomatic support at the United Nations, the administration reached an agreement with Port Moresby in August 1976, reintegrating into Papua New Guinea as an autonomous province. \n\n Status: Unrecognised secessionist state; Capital and largest settlement: Arawa; Official languages: English; Common languages: Tok Pisin; Government: Republic; Head of state: Alexis Sarei; Historical era: Decolonisation; Established: 1 September 1975; Disestablished: 9 August 1976; Succeeded by: Independent State of Papua New Guinea

name: Independent State of Papua New Guinea
description: The Independent State of Papua New Guinea attained sovereign statehood on 16 September 1975, terminating Australian administrative tutelage over the eastern half of New Guinea and its offshore archipelagos. Headquartered at Port Moresby on the southern Papuan coast, the constitutional monarchy recognised Queen Elizabeth II as head of state, with parliamentary governance directed by founding prime minister Sir Michael Somare. Encompassing immense linguistic diversity and rugged mountainous highlands, the Melanesian nation established a vibrant democratic tradition underpinned by mineral wealth, natural gas reserves and customary tribal landholding. \n\n Status: Commonwealth realm; Capital and largest city: Port Moresby; Official languages: English, Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu; Religion: Christianity; Government: Unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Head of state: Monarch of the United Kingdom; Legislature: National Parliament; Historical era: Contemporary; Currency: Kina

name: Republic of Indonesia (Military Occupation)
description: The Republic of Indonesia Military Occupation encompassed the former territory of Portuguese Timor following the covert armed incursions and full-scale invasion codenamed Operation Seroja in late 1975. Directed from Jakarta through regional military commands in Dili without recognised international legitimacy, the occupying authorities integrated the territory as the province of Timor Timur in 1976. Armed resistance led by Falintil and severe humanitarian privations characterised the occupation until a 1999 United Nations-supervised referendum overwhelmingly rejected Indonesian rule, culminating in the deployment of international peacekeepers in October 1999. \n\n Status: Military occupation administration; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Dili; Official languages: Indonesian; Common languages: Tetum and Portuguese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military administrative command; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 8 October 1975; Disestablished: 25 October 1999; Succeeded by: United Nations Transitional Administration in East Timor

name: People's Republic of Angola
description: The People's Republic of Angola was proclaimed on 11 November 1975 by the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola following the collapse of Portuguese colonial administration. Governed from Luanda under a Marxist-Leninist framework, the sovereign state immediately faced fierce opposition from rival insurgent factions in the protracted Angolan Civil War. Sustained by Cuban military assistance and Soviet diplomatic backing, the government defended its territory until signing the Bicesse Accords, which paved the way for constitutional multi-party governance in 1992. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Luanda; Official languages: Portuguese; Religion: State atheism; Government: Unitary Marxist-Leninist one-party republic; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 11 November 1975; Disestablished: 25 August 1992; Preceded by: Portuguese Angola; Succeeded by: Republic of Angola; Currency: Kwanza

name: Republic of Suriname
description: The Republic of Suriname achieved complete independence from the Kingdom of the Netherlands on 25 November 1975, establishing a sovereign republic along South America's north-eastern Atlantic seaboard. Governed from Paramaribo, the fledgling state maintained a diverse multi-ethnic society shaped by centuries of African and Asian migration alongside indigenous communities. Despite encountering political upheaval and military governance during the 1980s, the nation preserved its democratic parliamentary structures and rich tropical rainforest territory. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Paramaribo; Official languages: Dutch; Government: Unitary assembly-independent presidential republic; Legislature: National Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 25 November 1975; Preceded by: Surinam; Succeeded by: Republic of Suriname; Currency: Surinamese dollar

name: Democratic Republic of East Timor
description: The Democratic Republic of East Timor was proclaimed on 28 November 1975 by the Revolutionary Front for an Independent East Timor as Portuguese colonial rule collapsed across the eastern half of Timor. Headquartered at Dili, the infant sovereign state enjoyed only fleeting autonomy before Indonesian armed forces launched an amphibious invasion nine days later. The republican leadership withdrew into the rugged interior, maintaining armed guerrilla resistance against Indonesian occupation forces until their primary defensive bases were overwhelmed in 1979. \n\n Status: Partially recognised sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Dili; Official languages: Portuguese and Tetum; Government: Provisional republic; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 28 November 1975; Disestablished: 1 April 1979; Preceded by: Portuguese Timor; Succeeded by: Timor Timur; Currency: Portuguese Timorese escudo

name: People's Republic of Benin
description: The People's Republic of Benin was established on 30 November 1975 when military leader Mathieu Kerekou transformed the former Republic of Dahomey into a Marxist-Leninist state. Administered from Porto-Novo and the coastal commercial metropolis of Cotonou, the country was directed by the Vanguard People's Revolutionary Party of Benin through centralised economic planning and state secularism. Severe economic stagnation and popular unrest during the late 1980s eventually forced the regime to abandon communism in favour of multi-party constitutional rule in 1990. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Porto-Novo; Largest city: Cotonou; Official languages: French; Religion: State atheism; Government: Unitary Marxist-Leninist one-party republic; Legislature: Revolutionary National Assembly; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 30 November 1975; Disestablished: 1 March 1990; Preceded by: Republic of Dahomey; Succeeded by: Republic of Benin; Currency: West African CFA franc

name: Lao People's Democratic Republic
description: The Lao People's Democratic Republic was inaugurated on 2 December 1975 following the abdication of King Sisavang Vatthana and the decisive triumph of the communist Pathet Lao forces at the end of the Laotian Civil War. Operating from Vientiane as a landlocked single-party state along the Mekong River, the new administration consolidated power under the Lao People's Revolutionary Party while fostering close strategic bonds with neighbouring Vietnam. The country pursued collectivised agriculture and socialist development before adopting pragmatic market-oriented reforms during the late 1980s. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Vientiane; Official languages: Lao; Government: Unitary Marxist-Leninist one-party socialist republic; Legislature: National Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 2 December 1975; Preceded by: Kingdom of Laos; Currency: Kip

name: Islamic Republic of Mauritania (Military Occupation)
description: The Islamic Republic of Mauritania (Military Occupation) comprised the operational command and civil administration established over the southern sector of Western Sahara, known as Tiris al-Gharbiyya, following the 1975 Madrid Accords. Administered from Nouakchott, Mauritanian armed forces occupied key settlements including Dakhla while attempting to secure desert supply routes against the Polisario Front. Persistent guerrilla assaults and economic strain brought down the Mauritanian military regime, prompting a formal withdrawal and peace treaty in August 1979. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Nouakchott; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 20 December 1975; Disestablished: 14 August 1979; Preceded by: Spanish Sahara; Succeeded by: Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic; Currency: Mauritanian ouguiya

name: Democratic Republic of Madagascar
description: The Democratic Republic of Madagascar was instituted on 30 December 1975 after a national referendum approved a socialist constitution guided by naval officer Didier Ratsiraka. Governed from Antananarivo, the state embarked on extensive nationalisation of banking and industrial sectors under the ideological banner of the Charter of the Malagasy Socialist Revolution. Prolonged economic stagnation and escalating civilian demonstrations in the early 1990s ultimately dismantled the socialist framework, ushering in the Third Republic of Madagascar. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Antananarivo; Common languages: Malagasy and French; Government: Unitary socialist republic; Legislature: Popular National Assembly; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 30 December 1975; Disestablished: 12 January 1992; Preceded by: Malagasy Republic; Succeeded by: Republic of Madagascar; Currency: Malagasy franc

name: Colony of Tuvalu
description: The Colony of Tuvalu was constituted on 1 January 1976 as a distinct British Crown colony following the peaceful administrative separation of the Polynesian Ellice Islands from the Micronesian Gilbert Islands. Centred at Funafuti, the territory functioned under a resident commissioner and an elected House of Assembly representing nine low-lying atolls and reef islands. This transitional colonial administration focused on drafting a permanent democratic framework, which culminated in full sovereign independence within the Commonwealth in October 1978. \n\n Status: Crown colony of the United Kingdom; Capital: Funafuti; Official languages: English and Tuvaluan; Government: Constitutional monarchy under colonial administration; Head of state: Elizabeth II; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 1 January 1976; Disestablished: 1 October 1978; Preceded by: Gilbert and Ellice Islands; Succeeded by: Tuvalu; Currency: Australian dollar

name: Gilbert Islands
description: The Gilbert Islands operated as a self-governing British protectorate from 1976 to 1979 following the departure of the Ellice Islands from their previous shared colonial union. Centred at Bairiki on Tarawa atoll, the territory exercised internal legislative authority through a chief minister and council of ministers while external defence remained with the British Crown. The administration navigated economic transitions following the exhaustion of Ocean Island phosphate reserves before attaining full sovereign independence as the Republic of Kiribati in July 1979. \n\n Status: British protectorate; Capital: Bairiki; Official languages: English and Gilbertese; Government: Devolved parliamentary protectorate; Head of state: Elizabeth II; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 1 January 1976; Disestablished: 12 July 1979; Preceded by: Gilbert and Ellice Islands; Succeeded by: Republic of Kiribati; Currency: Australian dollar

name: Democratic Kampuchea
description: Democratic Kampuchea was the totalitarian communist state established across Cambodia by Pol Pot and the Khmer Rouge following their military takeover and the promulgation of a new constitution in January 1976. Centred nominally at Phnom Penh, the regime abolished modern commerce, currency and religious institutions, forcing the entire urban population into agrarian labour communes. An estimated quarter of the population perished from famine, exhaustion and systematic executions during the Cambodian genocide, which ended when Vietnamese armed forces captured the capital in early 1979. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Phnom Penh; Official languages: Khmer; Religion: State atheism; Government: Totalitarian communist dictatorship; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 5 January 1976; Disestablished: 1 April 1979; Preceded by: Khmer Republic; Succeeded by: People's Republic of Kampuchea; Currency: None (monetary system abolished)

name: People's Democratic Republic of Algeria (Military Occupation)
description: The People's Democratic Republic of Algeria (Military Occupation) comprised the forward tactical positions held by Algerian military units inside western sectors of Western Sahara during late January and February 1976. Operating without a fixed capital seat, these expeditionary detachments deployed near Amgala to deliver logistical assistance to the Sahrawi independence movement amid Spain's colonial withdrawal. Following severe conventional engagements against the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces, Algerian leadership withdrew its troops across the international boundary to bases around Tindouf. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile operational headquarters; Official languages: Modern Standard Arabic and French; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 20 January 1976; Disestablished: 27 February 1976; Preceded by: Spanish Sahara; Succeeded by: Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic; Currency: Algerian dinar

name: Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic
description: The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic was proclaimed by the Polisario Front on 27 February 1976 at Bir Lehlou as the last Spanish colonial authorities withdrew from Western Sahara. Claiming sovereignty over the entire territory, the republic governed the eastern interior Free Zone while managing sprawling refugee camps around Tindouf in neighbouring Algeria. Despite Morocco occupying the mineral-rich coastal regions, the Sahrawi state gained diplomatic recognition from dozens of sovereign nations and full membership in the African Union. \n\n Status: Partially recognised sovereign state; Capital: Bir Lehlou (provisional); Official languages: Arabic and Spanish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Semi-presidential one-party republic; Legislature: National Council; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 27 February 1976; Preceded by: Spanish Sahara; Currency: Sahrawi peseta

name: Socialist Republic of Vietnam
description: The Socialist Republic of Vietnam was proclaimed on 2 July 1976 through the formal reunification of North Vietnam and South Vietnam following the end of the Vietnam War. Governed from Hanoi by the Communist Party of Vietnam, the reunited state integrated the southern territories into a centralised socialist economic and administrative system. After surviving intense border conflicts and severe economic embargoes during the late 1970s, the nation embarked on market-oriented reforms known as Doi Moi, fostering rapid economic growth across Southeast Asia. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Hanoi; Largest city: Ho Chi Minh City; Official languages: Vietnamese; Government: Unitary Marxist-Leninist one-party socialist republic; Legislature: National Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 2 July 1976; Preceded by: Democratic Republic of Vietnam and Republic of South Vietnam; Currency: Vietnamese dong

name: Department of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon
description: The Department of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon functioned as an integral overseas department of France from July 1976 to June 1985, encompassing a small North Atlantic archipelago off Newfoundland. Centred at the port of Saint-Pierre, the administration was directed by a prefect appointed by Paris alongside a locally elected general council. Economic difficulties arising from metropolitan European customs duties on local fishing trade prompted the French government to reorganise the archipelago into an overseas territorial collectivity in 1985. \n\n Status: Overseas department of France; Capital: Saint-Pierre; Official languages: French; Government: Devolved departmental administration; Head of state: Valéry Giscard d'Estaing; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 19 July 1976; Disestablished: 11 June 1985; Preceded by: Territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon; Succeeded by: Territorial Collectivity of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon; Currency: French franc

name: Republic of Trinidad and Tobago
description: The Republic of Trinidad and Tobago was instituted on 1 August 1976 when the twin-island Caribbean nation adopted a republican constitution, replacing the British monarch with an elected ceremonial president. Governed from Port of Spain, the parliamentary republic utilised its abundant offshore petroleum and natural gas resources to build an industrialised energy and manufacturing economy. The state retained its Westminster-style parliamentary institutions, maintaining political stability and strong commercial integration within the wider Caribbean Community. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Port of Spain; Largest city: Chaguanas; Official languages: English; Government: Unitary parliamentary republic; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 1 August 1976; Preceded by: Trinidad and Tobago (Commonwealth realm); Currency: Trinidad and Tobago dollar

name: Central African Empire
description: The Central African Empire was established on 4 December 1976 when President Jean-Bedel Bokassa abolished the republican constitution and crowned himself Emperor Bokassa I in Bangui. The regime functioned as an autocratic military monarchy, bankrupting state finances with lavish imperial ceremonies while brutally suppressing political dissent. Growing international condemnation and internal atrocities culminated in a French-backed military intervention in September 1979, which deposed the emperor and restored the Central African Republic. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Bangui; Official languages: French and Sango; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Autocratic constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: Emperor; First ruler: Bokassa I; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 4 December 1976; Disestablished: 21 September 1979; Preceded by: Central African Republic; Succeeded by: Central African Republic; Currency: Central African CFA franc

name: Territorial Collectivity of Mayotte
description: The Territorial Collectivity of Mayotte was established on 24 December 1976 as a specialised overseas dependency of France after its inhabitants voted to remain under French sovereignty rather than join the newly independent Comoros. Administered from Mamoudzou on Grande-Terre, the Indian Ocean archipelago developed unique legal and administrative arrangements that respected traditional local customs while integrating French public law. The collectivity remained under this status until a popular referendum approved its elevation to a full overseas department in 2011. \n\n Status: Overseas collectivity of France; Administrative seat: Mamoudzou; Official languages: French; Common languages: Shimaore and Kibushi; Government: Devolved territorial collectivity; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 24 December 1976; Disestablished: 31 March 2011; Preceded by: Territory of the Comoro Islands; Succeeded by: Department of Mayotte; Currency: French franc and Euro

name: People's Socialist Republic of Albania
description: The People's Socialist Republic of Albania was established under the 1976 constitution, reaffirming the orthodox Marxist-Leninist course steered by Enver Hoxha and the Party of Labour of Albania. Administered from Tirana, the state pursued extreme political isolation, strict border militarisation, and mandated state atheism while severing its ideological alliance with China in 1978. Following Hoxha's death and escalating public demonstrations against economic scarcity, the communist regime collapsed in 1991, leading to the rebirth of a democratic republic. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Tirana; Official languages: Albanian; Religion: State atheism; Government: Unitary Hoxhaist communist one-party republic; Legislature: People's Assembly; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 28 December 1976; Disestablished: 28 April 1991; Preceded by: People's Republic of Albania; Succeeded by: Republic of Albania; Currency: Albanian lek

name: Argentine Republic (Military Occupation)
description: The Argentine Republic (Military Occupation) comprised the operational zones and naval outposts held by Argentine armed forces across South Atlantic islands, most prominently during the 1982 occupation of the Falkland Islands and South Georgia. Commanded by an expeditionary military governor based at Stanley, the occupying forces attempted to assert historic Argentine territorial claims against British sovereignty. The deployment provoked a decisive British military response in the Falklands War, culminating in Argentine capitulation in June 1982. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Stanley; Official languages: Spanish; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 1977; Disestablished: 20 June 1982; Preceded by: Falkland Islands and Dependencies; Succeeded by: Falkland Islands; Currency: Argentine peso

name: Namaland
label: bantustans
description: Namaland was established in 1977 as a segregated homeland for the Nama people within southern South West Africa under the apartheid policy enforced by South Africa. Administered from Keetmanshoop, the entity exercised limited local jurisdiction through a nominated tribal council before being reorganised into an ethnic representative authority in 1980. The homeland remained economically dependent on subsidies from Pretoria until its abolition in June 1989 as part of Namibia's transition to sovereign statehood. \n\n Status: Bantustan and ethnic representative authority; Capital: Keetmanshoop; Common languages: Nama, Afrikaans and English; Government: Apartheid tribal authority; Historical era: Late Cold War; Established: 1977; Disestablished: 1 June 1989; Preceded by: South West Africa; Succeeded by: Republic of Namibia; Currency: South African rand

name: Republic of Seychelles
description: The Republic of Seychelles entered a socialist era following a coup d'état in June 1977 that placed France-Albert Rene in executive power across the Indian Ocean archipelago. Governed from Victoria on the island of Mahe, the state instituted a one-party system led by the Seychelles People's Progressive Front, directing major investments toward universal health and primary education. In the early 1990s, constitutional revisions restored multi-party democracy while preserving the nation's high standard of living and expanding maritime conservation. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Victoria; Official languages: Seychellois Creole, English and French; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Legislature: National Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 5 June 1977; Preceded by: Republic of Seychelles; Currency: Seychellois rupee

name: KwaZulu
label: bantustans
description: KwaZulu was a semi-independent bantustan in north-eastern South Africa, designated by the apartheid authorities as the national homeland for the Zulu people. Headquartered at Ulundi under Chief Minister Mangosuthu Buthelezi, the territory rejected Pretoria's offer of full nominal independence to avoid forfeiting South African citizenship rights for its people. The fragmented territory functioned as an autonomous enclave throughout the twilight of apartheid until being completely reincorporated into KwaZulu-Natal province in April 1994. \n\n Status: Self-governing bantustan; Capital: Ulundi; Common languages: Zulu, English and Afrikaans; Government: Subnational parliamentary tribal authority; Head of state: Mangosuthu Buthelezi; Historical era: Late Cold War; Established: 1 February 1977; Disestablished: 27 April 1994; Preceded by: Republic of South Africa; Succeeded by: Republic of South Africa; Currency: South African rand

name: Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya
description: The Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya was proclaimed on 2 March 1977 by Muammar Gaddafi, establishing a novel system of direct popular rule rooted in his Third International Theory. Governed from Tripoli through basic people's congresses, the oil-wealthy North African state combined expansive welfare subsidies with an aggressive anti-Western foreign policy and interventions in regional civil wars. The long-standing authoritarian regime unraveled during the 2011 Libyan Civil War, culminating in the capture and death of Gaddafi. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Tripoli; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Jamahiriya; Ruler title: Brotherly Leader and Guide of the Revolution; First ruler: Muammar Gaddafi; Historical era: Cold War and post-Cold War; Established: 2 March 1977; Disestablished: 20 October 2011; Preceded by: Libyan Arab Republic; Succeeded by: State of Libya; Currency: Libyan dinar

name: Front for the National Liberation of the Congo
description: The Front for the National Liberation of the Congo was an armed insurgent movement formed by Katangese fighters who staged major cross-border military incursions into Zaire's Shaba province in 1977 and 1978. Operating from border encampments and briefly occupying the vital mining centre of Kolwezi, the rebel commanders sought the overthrow of President Mobutu Sese Seko. Their tactical advances threatened central government authority until combined French, Belgian and Moroccan expeditionary forces drove the insurgents back into Angola. \n\n Status: Insurgent quasi-state; Administrative seat: Kolwezi; Common languages: French and Swahili; Government: Rebel military administration; Head of state: Nathaniel Mbumba; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 10 March 1977; Disestablished: 1 July 1978; Preceded by: Republic of Zaire; Succeeded by: Republic of Zaire; Historical region: Katanga

name: Democratic Kampuchea (Military Occupation)
description: Democratic Kampuchea (Military Occupation) comprised the militarised border salients occupied by Khmer Rouge forces along the south-western frontier of Vietnam during violent incursions in 1977 and 1978. Operating without a fixed capital under orders from the high command in Phnom Penh, these armed detachments launched cross-border attacks into Vietnamese border villages across An Giang and Tay Ninh provinces. The incursions caused substantial civilian loss of life before prompt counter-strikes by the People's Army of Vietnam neutralised the occupied pockets. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile operational command; Official languages: Khmer; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 30 April 1977; Disestablished: 18 May 1978; Preceded by: Socialist Republic of Vietnam; Succeeded by: Socialist Republic of Vietnam; Currency: None (monetary system abolished)

name: Socialist Republic of Vietnam (Military Occupation)
description: The Socialist Republic of Vietnam (Military Occupation) encompassed the forward military operational zones held by the People's Army of Vietnam inside eastern Cambodia during recurrent border campaigns between 1977 and early 1979. Managed directly from tactical field headquarters, these operations aimed to suppress relentless Khmer Rouge cross-border assaults against Vietnamese frontier districts. The concentrated forward deployments eventually expanded into a full-scale offensive in December 1978, resulting in the capture of Phnom Penh and the installation of a friendly administration. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Forward field command; Official languages: Vietnamese; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 5 May 1977; Disestablished: 8 January 1979; Preceded by: Democratic Kampuchea; Succeeded by: People's Republic of Kampuchea; Currency: Vietnamese dong

name: Republic of Djibouti
description: The Republic of Djibouti emerged on 27 June 1977 after voters overwhelmingly endorsed sovereign independence from France, dissolving the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas. Positioned strategically on the Horn of Africa along the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, the republic maintained its capital at the historic port of Djibouti City. The country balanced political representation between the Afar and Issa Somali populations while developing its maritime infrastructure into a premier logistics gateway for the East African interior. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Djibouti; Official languages: Arabic and French; Common languages: Somali and Afar; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Legislature: National Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 27 June 1977; Preceded by: French Territory of the Afars and the Issas; Currency: Djiboutian franc

name: Somali Democratic Republic (Military Occupation)
description: The Somali Democratic Republic (Military Occupation) comprised the occupied territories of eastern Ethiopia held by the Somali National Army during the Ogaden War between July 1977 and March 1978. Administered through military expeditionary commands rather than a fixed civilian capital, Somali troops seized major urban centres including Gode and Jijiga in pursuit of a unified Greater Somalia. The occupation unraveled after Ethiopian armed forces, supported by massive Soviet equipment deliveries and Cuban combat units, launched a decisive counter-offensive that drove Somali units across the frontier. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Military field command; Official languages: Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 25 July 1977; Disestablished: 15 March 1978; Preceded by: Provisional Military Government of Socialist Ethiopia; Succeeded by: Provisional Military Government of Socialist Ethiopia; Currency: Somali shilling

name: Damaraland
label: bantustans
description: Damaraland was formed in 1978 as an ethnic bantustan in north-central South West Africa, designated by South African authorities to segregate the Damara population. Headquartered at Khorixas, the entity was granted an appointed representative council and limited autonomy over communal welfare under the framework of separate development. In 1980 it became a second-tier ethnic authority, continuing to function until all ethnic homelands were formally dissolved in 1989 ahead of the independence of Namibia. \n\n Status: Bantustan and ethnic representative authority; Capital: Khorixas; Common languages: Khoekhoe, Afrikaans, German and English; Government: Apartheid tribal authority; Historical era: Late Cold War; Established: 1978; Disestablished: 1 June 1989; Preceded by: South West Africa; Succeeded by: Republic of Namibia; Currency: South African rand

name: Rehoboth
label: bantustans
description: Rehoboth was an autonomous homeland created in 1978 in South West Africa to accommodate the Baster community, a distinct group descended from European settlers and indigenous southern Africans. Centred at the historic town of Rehoboth, the entity retained traditional governance structures including a Kaptein and an elected legislative assembly under South African oversight. The self-governing homeland preserved local property rights and land tenure systems until it was integrated into sovereign Namibia in 1989. \n\n Status: Bantustan and self-governing homeland; Capital: Rehoboth; Common languages: Afrikaans and English; Government: Apartheid homeland authority; Historical era: Late Cold War; Established: 1978; Disestablished: 1 June 1989; Preceded by: South West Africa; Succeeded by: Republic of Namibia; Currency: South African rand

name: Commonwealth of Dominica
description: The Commonwealth of Dominica became a fully sovereign parliamentary republic on 3 November 1978, severing its constitutional ties as an associated state of the United Kingdom. Situated in the Lesser Antilles between Guadeloupe and Martinique, the mountainous Caribbean island is governed from its coastal capital at Roseau. The nation maintained a stable democratic system and focused its economy on agricultural exports, geothermal exploration, and eco-tourism amid recurring tropical weather challenges. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Roseau; Official languages: English; Common languages: Dominican Creole French; Government: Unitary parliamentary republic; Legislature: House of Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 3 November 1978; Preceded by: West Indies Associated States; Currency: East Caribbean dollar

name: Democratic Republic of Afghanistan
description: The Democratic Republic of Afghanistan was founded on 30 April 1978 following the Saur Revolution, a military coup led by the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan that ousted President Mohammad Daoud Khan. Governed from Kabul, the Marxist-Leninist administration initiated radical social, agrarian and educational transformations that alienated conservative rural communities. Faced with escalating guerrilla rebellions across the countryside, the beleaguered government invited Soviet armed forces to intervene militarily in late 1979, triggering the protracted Soviet-Afghan War. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Kabul; Official languages: Pashto and Dari; Religion: State secularism; Government: Unitary socialist one-party republic; Ruler title: General Secretary; First ruler: Nur Muhammad Taraki; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 30 April 1978; Disestablished: 1 December 1987; Preceded by: Republic of Afghanistan; Succeeded by: Republic of Afghanistan; Currency: Afghan afghani

name: Solomon Islands
description: Solomon Islands achieved full sovereign statehood on 7 July 1978, concluding decades of British colonial rule and becoming an independent Commonwealth realm. Comprising six major islands and hundreds of smaller islets across Melanesia, the nation is governed from Honiara on Guadalcanal through a Westminster-style parliamentary democracy. The state concentrated on uniting its diverse provincial cultures while developing timber, fishing, and palm oil industries to sustain its expanding island population. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Honiara; Official languages: English; Common languages: Pijin; Government: Unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Head of state: Elizabeth II; Legislature: National Parliament; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 7 July 1978; Preceded by: British Solomon Islands; Currency: Solomon Islands dollar

name: Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka
description: The Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka adopted its modern constitutional identity on 7 September 1978, establishing an executive presidential system to guide the South Asian island nation. Governed from the executive centre of Colombo and the legislative seat of Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, the state enacted open-market economic reforms to modernise commerce. However, widening communal grievances between the Sinhalese majority and Tamil minority soon deteriorated into a devastating civil conflict that dominated subsequent decades. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Colombo and Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte; Official languages: Sinhala and Tamil; Government: Unitary semi-presidential republic; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 7 September 1978; Preceded by: Republic of Sri Lanka; Currency: Sri Lankan rupee

name: Tuvalu
description: Tuvalu gained full independence on 1 October 1978, emerging from British colonial rule as a sovereign microstate and constitutional monarchy within the Commonwealth. Administered from Funafuti across nine isolated atolls and reef islands in western Polynesia, the nation established a stable parliamentary democracy without formal political parties. The state developed revenue from traditional fisheries, philatelic sales, and internet domain licensing while actively championing global climate change initiatives. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Funafuti; Official languages: Tuvaluan and English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Head of state: Elizabeth II; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 1 October 1978; Preceded by: Colony of Tuvalu; Currency: Tuvaluan dollar and Australian dollar

name: Federal Islamic Republic of the Comoros
description: The Federal Islamic Republic of the Comoros was established on 23 October 1978 after a mercenary-backed coup returned Ahmed Abdallah to power, introducing an Islamic and federal constitution. Administered from Moroni on Grande Comore, the republic comprised three islands in the Mozambique Channel while asserting disputed claims over French-held Mayotte. The regime maintained controversial security connections with white-minority South Africa and suffered chronic political volatility until constitutional restructuring in 1999. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Moroni; Official languages: Comorian, French and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Federal Islamic presidential republic; Ruler title: President; First ruler: Ahmed Abdallah; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 23 October 1978; Disestablished: 30 April 1999; Preceded by: State of the Comoros; Succeeded by: Union of the Comoros; Currency: Comorian franc

name: Republic of Uganda (Military Occupation)
description: The Republic of Uganda (Military Occupation) existed from November 1978 to January 1979 when Ugandan military units invaded and occupied the Kagera Salient in northern Tanzania. Initiated by President Idi Amin, the expeditionary forces proclaimed the territory annexed to Uganda, looting infrastructure and displacing tens of thousands of local residents. The aggression triggered an overwhelming counter-offensive by the Tanzania People's Defence Force, which drove the Ugandan forces back across the border and ultimately ousted Amin in Kampala. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Military field command; Official languages: English and Swahili; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 1 November 1978; Disestablished: 5 January 1979; Preceded by: United Republic of Tanzania; Succeeded by: United Republic of Tanzania; Currency: Ugandan shilling

name: People's Republic of Kampuchea
description: The People's Republic of Kampuchea was proclaimed on 8 January 1979 following the capture of Phnom Penh by Vietnamese troops and Cambodian defectors, ousting the Khmer Rouge. Governed as a socialist client state supported by Hanoi and Moscow, the administration began the monumental task of rebuilding national institutions, schools, and health services in the wake of the Cambodian genocide. Despite governing most of the country, the regime faced diplomatic boycotts and ongoing guerrilla fighting until Vietnamese forces withdrew in 1989. \n\n Status: Protectorate and partially recognised socialist state; Capital and largest city: Phnom Penh; Official languages: Khmer; Religion: State secularism; Government: Unitary Marxist-Leninist one-party republic; Legislature: National Assembly; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 8 January 1979; Disestablished: 26 September 1989; Preceded by: Democratic Kampuchea; Succeeded by: State of Cambodia; Currency: Kampuchean riel

name: Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (Military Occupation)
description: The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (Military Occupation) comprised the operational zone briefly seized by Polisario Front guerrillas inside the southern Moroccan city of Tan-Tan in late January 1979. Launched as a swift desert raid during the Western Sahara War, the fighters overran military checkpoints and held municipal outposts to demonstrate their operational reach beyond the disputed territory. The insurgent forces inflicted structural damage and captured supplies before withdrawing into the desert hinterland three days later. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile operational command; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Revolutionary insurgent administration; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 28 January 1979; Disestablished: 31 January 1979; Preceded by: Kingdom of Morocco; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Morocco; Currency: Sahrawi peseta

name: United Republic of Tanzania (Military Occupation)
description: The United Republic of Tanzania (Military Occupation) encompassed southern and central regions of Uganda occupied by the Tanzania People's Defence Force between February and June 1979 during the Kagera War. Deployed under the command of Tanzanian military officers alongside allied Ugandan rebel groups, the forces advanced systematically northward to capture towns such as Masaka, Mbarara, and Kampala. The operational administration maintained civil order and secured infrastructure until authority was transferred to the newly formed Uganda National Liberation Front. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile field command; Official languages: Swahili and English; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 11 February 1979; Disestablished: 3 June 1979; Preceded by: Republic of Uganda; Succeeded by: Uganda National Liberation Front; Currency: Tanzanian shilling

name: Saint Lucia
description: Saint Lucia achieved full sovereign statehood on 22 February 1979, becoming an independent constitutional monarchy and Commonwealth realm in the eastern Caribbean. Located in the Windward Islands between Martinique and Saint Vincent, the island nation is governed from its coastal capital of Castries. The country fostered a stable parliamentary democracy, expanding from its historical agricultural base in sugar and bananas into high-end international tourism and light manufacturing. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Castries; Official languages: English; Common languages: Saint Lucian Creole French; Government: Unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Head of state: Elizabeth II; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 22 February 1979; Preceded by: West Indies Associated States; Currency: East Caribbean dollar

name: Islamic Republic of Iran
description: The Islamic Republic of Iran was inaugurated on 1 April 1979 following a national referendum that abolished the monarchy in the culmination of the Iranian Revolution. Guided by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the state established a theocratic political framework in Tehran that integrated clerical oversight with an elected presidency and parliament. The fledgling republic defended its borders during the brutal eight-year Iran-Iraq War while asserting an influential, independent foreign policy across the Middle East. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Tehran; Official languages: Persian; Religion: Twelver Shia Islam; Government: Unitary theocratic presidential Islamic republic; Head of state: Supreme Leader; Legislature: Islamic Consultative Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 1 April 1979; Preceded by: Imperial State of Iran; Currency: Iranian rial

name: Greenland
description: Greenland attained devolved home-rule status within the Kingdom of Denmark on 1 May 1979 following an overwhelming affirmative vote by its electorate. Governed from its capital at Nuuk, the vast Arctic island took control of internal legislation, environmental stewardship, and taxation through its elected parliament, the Inatsisartut. In 1982, the self-governing territory voted to withdraw from the European Economic Community to safeguard its vital fishing grounds and cultural heritage. \n\n Status: Autonomous constituent territory of Denmark; Capital and largest city: Nuuk; Official languages: Greenlandic; Common languages: Danish; Government: Devolved parliamentary system under constitutional monarchy; Legislature: Inatsisartut; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 1 May 1979; Preceded by: Greenland (Danish province); Currency: Danish krone

name: Zimbabwe Rhodesia
description: Zimbabwe Rhodesia was established on 1 June 1979 as an unrecognised state resulting from the Internal Settlement between Ian Smith's administration and moderate African nationalists. Centred at Salisbury under Prime Minister Abel Muzorewa, the state abolished minority rule and created a black-majority government, yet failed to secure international diplomatic recognition or halt the bush war. Faced with persistent insurgent warfare and international sanctions, the administration concluded the Lancaster House Agreement in December 1979, voluntarily reverting to British colonial oversight. \n\n Status: Unrecognised sovereign state; Capital: Salisbury; Official languages: English; Common languages: Shona and Sindebele; Government: Parliamentary republic; Head of state: Josiah Zion Gumede; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 1 June 1979; Disestablished: 12 December 1979; Preceded by: Republic of Rhodesia; Succeeded by: Southern Rhodesia; Currency: Rhodesian dollar

name: Republic of Kiribati
description: The Republic of Kiribati gained sovereign statehood on 12 July 1979, uniting thirty-three coral atolls and reef islands across Micronesia and Polynesia upon independence from the United Kingdom. Headquartered at South Tarawa with administrative facilities at Bairiki, the Pacific nation instituted an executive presidency integrated directly into its unicameral parliament. The island republic manages vast oceanic fisheries within its exclusive economic zone while taking an active diplomatic stance against the perils of rising global sea levels. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Bairiki; Largest city: South Tarawa; Official languages: English and Gilbertese; Government: Unitary parliamentary republic with an executive president; Legislature: House of Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 12 July 1979; Preceded by: Gilbert Islands; Currency: Australian dollar

name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
description: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines became an independent sovereign nation and Commonwealth realm on 27 October 1979, terminating its status as a British associated state in the eastern Caribbean. Centred at Kingstown on the principal island of Saint Vincent, the multi-island country exercises authority over thirty-two smaller islands in the northern Grenadines chain. The parliamentary democracy developed an economy historically rooted in banana cultivation and agricultural trade, diversifying into marine services and tourism. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Kingstown; Official languages: English; Government: Unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Head of state: Elizabeth II; Legislature: House of Assembly; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 27 October 1979; Preceded by: Saint Vincent; Currency: East Caribbean dollar

name: Colony of Southern Rhodesia
description: The Colony of Southern Rhodesia was briefly reconstituted on 12 December 1979 under the Lancaster House Agreement, peacefully terminating the unrecognised regime of Zimbabwe Rhodesia. Governed from Salisbury by British governor Lord Soames, the transitional colonial authority managed a general ceasefire among combatants and supervised universal democratic elections. The administration brought an orderly end to the Rhodesian Bush War, transferring full sovereign independence to the Republic of Zimbabwe on 18 April 1980. \n\n Status: Crown colony of the United Kingdom; Capital: Salisbury; Official languages: English; Common languages: Shona and Sindebele; Government: Direct colonial administration under constitutional monarchy; Head of state: Elizabeth II; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 12 December 1979; Disestablished: 18 April 1980; Preceded by: Zimbabwe Rhodesia; Succeeded by: Republic of Zimbabwe; Currency: Rhodesian dollar

name: People's Revolutionary Republic of Guinea
description: The People's Revolutionary Republic of Guinea constituted the final ideological phase of Ahmed Sekou Toure's regime from 1980 until his death in 1984. Centred at Conakry, the West African socialist state operated under the monopolistic authority of the Democratic Party of Guinea, aligning closely with Eastern Bloc partners. Beset by severe economic shortages and political repression, the revolutionary governance model was abruptly dissolved on 3 April 1984 when the military seized power in a bloodless coup. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Conakry; Official languages: French; Government: Unitary socialist one-party republic; Ruler title: President; First ruler: Ahmed Sékou Touré; Historical era: Cold War; Established: 1980; Disestablished: 3 April 1984; Preceded by: Republic of Guinea; Succeeded by: Republic of Guinea; Currency: Guinean syli

name: Republic of Zimbabwe
description: The Republic of Zimbabwe emerged as a globally recognised sovereign state on 18 April 1980 following the conclusion of the Rhodesian Bush War and internationally supervised elections. Governed from Harare under the leadership of Robert Mugabe and ZANU-PF, the landlocked nation made rapid early strides in public healthcare and primary education. The country later encountered economic crises, contentious land redistribution programmes, and severe currency instability, whilst preserving its parliamentary and presidential institutions. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Harare; Official languages: English, Shona and Sindebele; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 18 April 1980; Preceded by: Southern Rhodesia; Currency: Zimbabwean dollar and US dollar

name: Republic of Vanuatu
description: The Republic of Vanuatu attained sovereign independence on 30 July 1980, bringing an end to seven decades of shared Anglo-French condominium rule over the New Hebrides. Centred at Port-Vila on Efate island, the archipelagic Melanesian state instituted a parliamentary republic that embraced Bislama, English, and French as official languages. The nation drew strength from indigenous custom and decentralised island councils, building a growing economy around cattle ranching, copra cultivation, and eco-tourism. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital and largest city: Port-Vila; Official languages: Bislama, English and French; Government: Unitary parliamentary republic; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Contemporary; Established: 30 July 1980; Preceded by: New Hebrides; Currency: Vatu

name: Bushmanland
label: bantustans
description: Bushmanland was an apartheid bantustan established in 1981 in eastern South West Africa to segregate the San populations under South African colonial rule. Managed without a formal urban capital from the administrative settlement of Tsumkwe, the remote territory lacked genuine self-governing institutions and remained heavily reliant on external colonial administrators. The homeland provided minimal civil infrastructure until it was permanently abolished in June 1989 during the transition towards an independent Namibia. \n\n Status: Bantustan; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Tsumkwe; Common languages: San languages, Afrikaans and English; Government: Apartheid territorial administration; Historical era: Late Cold War; Established: 1981; Disestablished: 1 June 1989; Preceded by: South West Africa; Succeeded by: Republic of Namibia; Currency: South African rand

name: Kaokoland
label: bantustans
description: Kaokoland was established in 1981 in north-western South West Africa as an apartheid homeland designated for the Ovahimba and related pastoralist groups. Centred at Opuwo, the rugged and arid territory never received an autonomous legislative assembly, functioning instead under the direct administrative oversight of neighbouring Hereroland authorities. The sparsely populated enclave remained under colonial control until all ethnic homelands were disbanded in 1989, subsequently becoming part of Namibia's Kunene Region. \n\n Status: Bantustan; Capital: Opuwo; Common languages: Otjiherero, Afrikaans and English; Government: Apartheid territorial administration; Historical era: Late Cold War; Established: 1981; Disestablished: 1 June 1989; Preceded by: South West Africa; Succeeded by: Republic of Namibia; Currency: South African rand

name: Republic of Palau
description: The Republic of Palau operated as a self-governing dependency under United States trusteeship from 1981 to 1994 after opting not to join the Federated States of Micronesia. Headquartered at Koror, the western Pacific archipelago enacted its own constitution and elected a national congress to guide local domestic legislation. After extensive bilateral discussions regarding security compacts and environmental safeguards, the territory attained full sovereign independence in free association with Washington in October 1994. \n\n Status: United States dependency and UN trust territory; Capital: Koror; Official languages: Palauan and English; Government: Unitary presidential constitutional dependency; Legislature: Palau National Congress; Historical era: Late Cold War; Established: 1 January 1981; Disestablished: 1 October 1994; Preceded by: Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands; Succeeded by: Republic of Palau; Currency: United States dollar

name: Saint Christopher and Nevis
description: Saint Christopher and Nevis functioned as an internally self-governing British associated state between 1981 and 1983 following the formal separation of Anguilla from the colonial union. Governed from Basseterre on Saint Kitts under Premier Kennedy Simmonds, the administration exercised complete domestic legislative power while Britain remained responsible for defence and diplomacy.
